images.title: Endocrine Glands
images.caption: The endocrine glands release hormones straight into the blood. Crin/o means to secrete: endocrine glands secrete inward, into the blood, and exocrine glands secrete outward through ducts.
images.alt: Female and male body outlines showing the endocrine glands: pineal and pituitary glands in the brain, thyroid and parathyroid glands in the neck, adrenal glands on the kidneys, pancreas, ovaries and testes.
images.credit: OpenStax & Tomáš Kebert & umimeto.org, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Digestive Tract
images.caption: Food passes from the mouth through the pharynx, esophagus (Esophag/o) and stomach (Gastr/o) into the small intestine (Enter/o). The liver (Hepat/o), gallbladder and pancreas add digestive juices.
images.alt: Front view of the digestive system from the mouth to the rectum, showing the salivary glands, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine and appendix.
images.credit: Mariana Ruiz, Jmarchn, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Layers of the Skin
images.caption: Derm/o, Dermat/o and Cutane/o all mean skin. The epidermis is the outer layer, the dermis below it holds glands, hair follicles and nerves, and the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) stores fat.
images.alt: Cut-away block of skin showing the epidermis, dermis and hypodermis, with hair shafts and follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, arrector pili muscle, blood vessels, nerves and fat.
images.credit: OpenStax College : J. Gordon Betts, Peter Desaix, Eddie Johnson, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Parts of a Cell
images.caption: Cyt/o means cell. The nucleus holds the genetic material, and the organelles in the cytoplasm make energy (mitochondria), build proteins (ribosomes, rough ER) and package them (Golgi apparatus).
images.alt: Cut-away drawing of an animal cell showing the nucleus, nucleolus, nuclear envelope, mitochondria, ribosomes, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosome, peroxisome, centrosome, secretory vesicle, cytoplasm and plasma membrane.

images.title: Structure of a Tooth
images.caption: Dent/o and Odont/o mean tooth, and Gingiv/o means gums. Hard enamel covers the crown, dentin forms the body of the tooth, and the pulp in the middle holds the nerves and blood vessels that run up through the root canal.
images.alt: Cut-away of a molar in the jaw showing the enamel, dentin, pulp, root canal, gingiva, cementum, jaw bone and root apex, with brackets marking the crown, neck and root.

images.title: Types of Permanent Teeth
images.caption: Adults have 32 permanent teeth. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind food. The upper teeth sit in the maxilla and the lower teeth in the mandible.
images.alt: Open mouth showing the upper and lower rows of permanent teeth, with the incisors, canines, premolars and molars marked on each row.
images.credit: Gregory david baker, Vectorization:  Mrmw, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Bones of the Skull (Front View)
images.caption: Crani/o refers to the skull. The upper jaw is the maxilla and the lower jaw is the mandible, the only movable bone of the skull. The teeth are anchored in these two bones.
images.alt: Front view of the skull with each bone in a different colour: frontal, parietal, temporal, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, nasal and zygomatic bones, the maxilla and the mandible.
images.credit: LadyofHats (Mariana Ruiz Villarreal), via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Body Planes and Axes
images.caption: The sagittal plane divides the body into right and left parts, the coronal (frontal) plane into front and back, and the transverse plane into upper and lower parts.
images.alt: Standing figure cut by three planes: a sagittal plane, a coronal plane and a transverse plane, with dotted lines for the craniocaudal, left-right and anteroposterior axes.

images.title: Synovial Joint
images.caption: Arthr/o means joint and Chondr/o means cartilage. In a synovial joint, articular cartilage covers the bone ends, and synovial fluid inside the joint capsule lets the bones glide.
images.alt: Cross-section of a knee-type synovial joint showing the synovial cavity, joint capsule, articular cartilage, bursa, tendon, ligament, epiphyseal bone and the extensor and flexor muscles, with the proximal and distal bones marked.

images.title: The Human Skeleton
images.caption: The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum) forms the body's central axis. The appendicular skeleton includes the limbs, shoulder girdle and pelvis. Oste/o means bone.
images.alt: Front view of the whole human skeleton with the skull, clavicle, scapula, sternum, ribs, humerus, vertebral column, ulna, radius, pelvis, femur, patella, tibia and fibula marked.
images.credit: LadyofHats (Mariana Ruiz Villarreal), via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Structure of a Long Bone
images.caption: A long bone has a shaft (diaphysis) and two ends (epiphyses). Hard compact bone forms the outer wall, while spongy bone fills the ends. The medullary cavity in the shaft holds bone marrow (Myel/o).
images.alt: A femur with one end cut open, showing spongy bone, compact bone and the medullary cavity, with brackets marking the epiphyses, metaphyses and diaphysis.

images.title: Blood Flow Through the Heart
images.caption: Blood from the body enters the right atrium, goes through the right ventricle to the lungs, returns to the left atrium and is pumped out of the left ventricle into the aorta. Cardi/o means heart.
images.alt: Circular flow diagram with arrows showing the path of blood: from the body tissues through the right side of the heart to the lungs, then back through the left side of the heart to the aorta and body. All 14 step labels are blank.
images.license: User-supplied course material (not openly licensed; internal course use only)
images.note: The labeled version is the original course image with the same crop.

images.title: Structures of the Heart
images.caption: The heart has four chambers (two atria and two ventricles) and four valves that keep blood flowing one way. The wall has three layers: endocardium, myocardium and epicardium.
images.alt: Cutaway front view of the heart showing its four chambers, valves, septa, great vessels and wall layers, with 21 blank labels connected to the structures by leader lines.
images.license: User-supplied course material (not openly licensed; internal course use only)
images.note: The labeled version is the original course image with the same crop.

images.title: Electrical Conduction System
images.caption: Each heartbeat starts at the SA node, the pacemaker. The signal passes to the AV node, then down the bundle of His and the bundle branches to the Purkinje fibers.
images.alt: Cutaway drawing of the heart with the conduction system highlighted: the SA node in the right atrium, internodal pathways, the AV node, the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers in the ventricle walls. The four chambers are also marked. All 11 labels are blank.
images.credit: Drj (CardioNetworks); blank version by YitzhakNat, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The labeled version has the answers drawn into the blank label areas.

images.title: Coronary Arteries
images.caption: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself. A blockage in one of them causes a myocardial infarction (heart attack).
images.alt: Front view of the heart showing the right coronary artery and the left coronary artery with its branches on the heart's surface, along with the great vessels and chambers. All 14 labels are blank.
images.credit: Patrick J. Lynch, Fred the Oyster, Mikael Häggström, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The labeled version has the answers drawn into the blank label areas.

images.title: Blood Vessels
images.caption: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it back. Gas exchange happens in the tiny capillaries between the arterioles and the venules. Angi/o and Vas/o mean vessel.
images.alt: Diagram of an artery carrying blood from the heart, branching into arterioles, a capillary network and venules, which join a vein that returns blood to the heart. Cutaways show the layers of the artery wall and a valve inside the vein, and a close-up of a capillary shows a red blood cell. All 13 labels are blank.
images.note: The labeled version has the answers drawn into the blank label areas.

images.title: Blood Cells (Hematopoiesis)
images.caption: Hem/o and Hemat/o mean blood. Bone marrow makes erythrocytes (red cells), thrombocytes (platelets, from megakaryocytes) and leukocytes (white cells): neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes and lymphocytes.
images.alt: Family tree of blood cells formed in bone marrow, showing the erythrocyte, megakaryocyte and thrombocytes, the neutrophil, eosinophil and basophil, the monocyte and macrophage, and the lymphocytes (B and T cells, plasma cell and natural killer cell).
images.credit: A. Rad and Mikael Häggström, M.D. Author info - Reusing images- Conflicts of interest:  None, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Lymphatic System
images.caption: Lymph/o means lymph. Lymph vessels carry fluid back to the blood through the thoracic duct, and lymph nodes filter it along the way. The thymus (Thym/o) and spleen (Splen/o) are lymphatic organs.
images.alt: Female body outline with green lymph vessels and clusters of lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, abdomen, pelvis and groin, plus the thoracic duct, cisterna chyli, thymus and spleen.

images.title: Structure of a Lymph Node
images.caption: Lymph enters a node through afferent vessels and leaves through efferent vessels. Inside, the cortex and medulla filter the lymph, and lymphocytes trap germs.
images.alt: Cut-away of a bean-shaped lymph node with afferent lymphatic vessels entering and efferent vessels leaving, showing the capsule, cortex, nodules, sinuses, medulla and valves.
images.credit: Lennert B (original); Tamil derivative by Commons user sibi, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Alveoli
images.caption: Alveol/o means air sac. Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
images.alt: Close-up of grape-like clusters of alveoli at the end of a bronchiole, with the alveolar duct, alveolar sacs, pulmonary artery and vein branches and capillary beds around them.

images.title: Regions of the Pharynx
images.caption: The pharynx (throat, Pharyng/o) has three parts: the nasopharynx behind the nose, the oropharynx behind the mouth (Or/o), and the laryngopharynx above the larynx.
images.alt: Side view of the head cut down the middle, with the nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx marked, plus the nasal cavity, hard palate and tongue.

images.title: The Respiratory Tract
images.caption: Air flows through the nasal cavity (Nas/o, Rhin/o), pharynx (Pharyng/o), larynx (Laryng/o) and trachea (Trache/o) into the bronchi (Bronch/o), which branch into the lungs (Pneum/o, Pulmon/o). The right lung has three lobes and the left has two.
images.alt: Front view of the respiratory system showing the nasal cavity, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, carina, right and left main bronchi, the three lobes of the right lung, the two lobes of the left lung, and the diaphragm.
images.credit: Bibi Saint-Pol, Jmarchn, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Lobes of the Brain
images.caption: The cerebrum (Cerebr/o) is divided into the frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. The cerebellum (Cerebell/o) sits at the back and coordinates balance and movement.
images.alt: Side view of the brain with each lobe in a different colour: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, plus the cerebellum and brainstem.
images.credit: Cancer Research UK, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Meninges
images.caption: Mening/o means membrane. The three meninges cover the brain and spinal cord: the tough dura mater on the outside, the arachnoid in the middle, and the delicate pia mater on the brain surface.
images.alt: Cut-away from the scalp down to the brain showing the skin, aponeurosis, periosteum and bone, then the dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater, with a dural venous sinus and an arachnoid granulation.
images.credit: Mysid (SVG), SEER Development Team (original), Jmarchn, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Brain: Midsagittal View
images.caption: The thalamus (Thalam/o) relays sensory signals, and the hypothalamus below it controls body temperature, hunger and hormones. The brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata) connects the brain to the spinal cord (Myel/o).
images.alt: Brain cut down the middle showing the cerebrum, corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum and the highlighted brainstem: mesencephalon, pons and medulla oblongata, continuing into the spinal cord.
images.credit: Patrick J. Lynch, variation by User:Hk kng, via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Structure of a Neuron
images.caption: Neur/o means nerve. A neuron receives signals through its dendrites, and the cell body (with its nucleus) passes them along the axon to the axon terminals. Schwann cells form the myelin sheath that speeds the signal.
images.alt: A neuron with branching dendrites, a cell body with its nucleus, and a long axon wrapped in myelin sheath segments formed by Schwann cells, separated by nodes of Ranvier, ending in axon terminals.

images.title: Central vs Peripheral Nervous System
images.caption: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain (Encephal/o) and spinal cord (Myel/o). The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is the nerves and ganglia (clusters of nerve cell bodies) that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.
images.alt: Body outline showing the brain and spinal cord as the central nervous system, and nerves and ganglia branching out as the peripheral nervous system.
